one_line: Rustem Feyzkhanov (Snorkel AI) on turning production agent traces into repeatable, containerized simulation benchmarks that serve as release gates and training data.
summary: The speaker argues every company shipping agents needs a private benchmark that mimics its real tools, APIs, policies and workflows, because public benchmarks only orient and private ones let you ship. Raw production traces are good for finding failures but hard to compare, since database state and tool versions drift between runs. The fix is to build tasks from traces and run them as offline simulations, scoring cost, latency and retries alongside pass rate. A task is a Harbor-style folder: an instruction file, a Docker environment, a hidden oracle solution, verifiers and metadata. The environment is a mini production made of sidecar containers with mocked APIs and an LLM-simulated user, and long tasks are split into steps with their own verifiers that can stop early. Verifiers check the final environment state, using deterministic checks plus LLM or agent judges, with subject-matter experts reviewing only cases where the judges disagree with the agent. Benchmarks are treated as software, with their own CI that checks pinned dependencies, runs the oracle, and tags difficulty by agent success rate. The improvement loop feeds production failures back into the benchmark and fixes problems in the right layer (prompt, skill or structured output) instead of piling rules into the prompt.

key_ideas.idea: Every company needs a private benchmark; public ones only orient
key_ideas.detail: Public benchmarks (SWE-bench, Terminal-bench, OSWorld-style) target specific domains and mostly report pass rate. A private benchmark matches your domain, tools, policies and production environment, and is what you use to ship.

key_ideas.idea: Turn production traces into repeatable experiments
key_ideas.detail: Traces show input, actions and output and are good for finding failures, but A/B tests on live traffic are not apples to apples because database state and tool versions change. Building tasks from traces lets you replay them offline under different agent configs and compare cost, latency and retries, not just pass rate.

key_ideas.idea: Evaluate the whole system, not just the model
key_ideas.detail: The speaker's list of knobs includes the model's thinking level, the prompt, the harness, skills and the tool set. The environment and evaluators stay fixed between runs so only the system under test changes.

key_ideas.idea: A benchmark task has a fixed anatomy, and the oracle proves it is solvable
key_ideas.detail: The Harbor layout has an instruction markdown file the agent sees, a Dockerfile or compose file for the environment, and a hidden oracle solution and verifiers, plus metadata. The oracle runs the same pipeline with a scripted solution instead of the agent, to confirm the task can be solved at all.

key_ideas.idea: The environment should be mini-production, and the user should be simulated
key_ideas.detail: Use the same database, APIs, tools and files as production, but as snapshots. Run API services, databases and MCP tools as sidecar containers, mock what is expensive, and replace real users with an LLM that has its own persona prompt. The agent should not be able to tell it is in a simulation.

key_ideas.idea: Long-horizon tasks need step-level prompts and verifiers
key_ideas.detail: Split a multi-hour task into intermediate steps, each with its own prompt and verifiers. The run can end early when the agent is clearly failing, which saves cost.

key_ideas.idea: Verify the final environment state, not only the output text
key_ideas.detail: The verifier reads the final database state, API responses and output artifacts, not just the answer. Use deterministic checks where possible (tool calls, final values), LLM or agent judges for trace quality and planning, and SME review only on disagreements.

key_ideas.idea: Treat the benchmark as software with its own CI
key_ideas.detail: Check pinned dependencies and base images and missing fixtures. Run the oracle (or confirm verifiers fail without it), run several agent attempts to confirm the task is solvable but hard, tag it simple, medium or hard by success rate, and only then approve it into the suite.

key_ideas.idea: Fix failures in the right layer, not by stacking prompt rules
key_ideas.detail: Anti-pattern: piling 'never do X / critical: Y' into the prompt. With the full stack under simulation, context overload is fixed by changing the harness, a missing procedure goes into a skill, and an output contract goes into structured output. Change one thing, rerun the full benchmark, then release.

key_ideas.idea: Run two loops that share one data pipeline: benchmark expansion and release gating
key_ideas.detail: Loop one pulls failures from observability traces into the benchmark. Loop two runs the simulation runner on the extended benchmark for each new config and uses the result as a release gate. The speaker says observability and experimentation are two sides of the same coin and should be connected.

techniques.name: Trace-to-task conversion
techniques.how: Take production traces, extract the input, the environment state and the expected outcome, and turn each into a containerized task with an oracle and verifiers. Keep the database snapshot and tool versions pinned so runs are repeatable.
techniques.when: When production failures need to be reproduced and compared across agent configs, and A/B tests on live traffic are too noisy.

techniques.name: Harbor-style task folder
techniques.how: One folder per task: instruction.md (what the agent sees), environment/ (Dockerfile or compose), solution/ (oracle, hidden from the agent), tests/ or verifiers, and task metadata. The speaker presents this as the common format from the team behind Terminal-bench.
techniques.when: When you want a portable, repeatable unit for an agent benchmark that can run in parallel.

techniques.name: Oracle-first validation
techniques.how: Write a scripted oracle solution and run it through the same pipeline to confirm the verifiers pass. If the oracle fails, the task is broken, not the agent.
techniques.when: Before any agent run on a new task, to separate task bugs from agent failures.

techniques.name: Sidecar service mocking with a simulated user
techniques.how: Run the agent in a main container and put databases, mocked API services and MCP tools in sidecar containers. A simulated user is an LLM with a persona prompt that drives the conversation.
techniques.when: When the real production services or real users cannot be used in an experiment, but the agent must not know it is in a sandbox.

techniques.name: Stepwise long-horizon simulation
techniques.how: Split a long task into steps, each with its own prompt and verifier. Stop the simulation early when a step fails.
techniques.when: For multi-hour agent workflows where a late failure would waste a full run.

techniques.name: Layered verifiers with SME escalation
techniques.how: Combine deterministic checks on final state and tool calls with LLM or agent judges for planning and trace quality. Route only the cases where the agent and the verifiers disagree to subject-matter experts.
techniques.when: When full human review is too costly but the team still needs human judgement on borderline cases.

techniques.name: Benchmark CI and difficulty tagging
techniques.how: Run lint-style checks (pinned deps, base images, fixtures), run the oracle, run several agent attempts, tag each task by its success rate, and approve tasks into the suite only after they pass.
techniques.when: When the benchmark is shared by several teams or used as a release gate, so that broken tasks do not skew results.

techniques.name: Coverage split: happy path plus edge cases
techniques.how: Build bread-and-butter tasks for the main workflows and also tasks where tools fail or the database misbehaves, in the style of integration tests.
techniques.when: When designing the task distribution for an agent that must survive production failures.

techniques.name: Held-out split for agent config
techniques.how: Keep a standalone set the agent configs never see during experimentation, similar to a classic train/test split. The speaker offers roughly 80/20 as a starting point.
techniques.when: When tuning agent configs against a benchmark, to avoid overfitting to it.

tools: Arize (experiment and trace recording; transcript says 'Arise')

numbers.claim: Snorkel runs millions of agent simulations per month
Speaker's rule of thumb for a train/validation split is roughly 80/20, depending on the use case
Tasks are tagged simple, medium or hard by how often the agent succeeds across several runs (no thresholds given)

Speaker references a case where a small open model was fine-tuned on simulation traces to match a large model's performance on a specific task (no numbers given in the talk; details are on Snorkel's website)

hot_takes: Every company that ships agents needs its own benchmark; public benchmarks only help you orient.
A benchmark is software: it needs code review, pinned dependencies and its own CI pipeline.
Traces find production edge cases, but only simulation tells you what would happen under a changed config.
Stacking prompt rules like 'never do X' is an anti-pattern; fix context overload in the harness, missing procedures in skills, and output shape in structured output.
Benchmarks should feed training, not only evaluation: the same traces can fine-tune a smaller model.

relevance.why: AgentOS's stated next-phase thesis is proving the system with benchmarks and correctness checks, and this talk gives a concrete task format (Harbor-style folder, oracle, verifiers, sidecar mocks) for doing that across its layers.
relevance.action: Prototype one Harbor-style task for the InferCraft or MemoryMesh path with a Docker environment, an oracle solution, and a verifier that checks final state, and run it through the existing RAGAS and Locust setup to see whether cost, latency and retries can be compared across configs.

relevance.why: ProsHarness's checkpoint/resume and plan-critique loop could be tested with step-level verifiers, but the talk does not cover harness checkpointing.
relevance.action: Look at whether a ProsHarness run can be split into steps with per-step verifiers so an early failure stops the run, the way the speaker describes.

relevance.why: Treating benchmarks as CI-checked software, with oracle runs, multi-attempt difficulty tagging and a held-out split, applies to any eval suite the user builds for agents.
relevance.action: Add a CI check for any eval task that runs its oracle or reference solution first and fails the build if the oracle does not pass, then tag tasks by agent success rate over several runs.
